entries.ae638277bcfd9dcd8f641cb22ca37269d6bdec1f: <div sID="gen9504" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Job.12" sID="Job.12"/> <div eID="gen9504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9505" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9506" type="x-p"/> In this and the two following chapters we have Job's answer to Zophar's discourse, in which, as before, he first reasons with his friends (see <reference osisRef="Job.13.19">ch. xiii. 19</reference>) and then turns to his God, and directs his expostulations to him, from thence to the end of his discourse. In this chapter he addresses himself to his friends, and, I. He condemns what they had said of him, and the judgment they had given of his character, <reference osisRef="Job.12.1-Job.12.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He contradicts and confronts what they had said of the destruction of wicked people in this world, showing that they often prosper, <reference osisRef="Job.12.6-Job.12.11">ver. 6-11</reference>. III. He consents to what they had said of the wisdom, power, and sovereignty of God, and the dominion of his providence over the children of men and all their affairs; he confirms this, and enlarges upon it, <reference osisRef="Job.12.12-Job.12.25">ver. 12-25</reference>.
entries.c17430261e71b71f331e23a29821d325a5532a10: <div eID="gen9506" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9505" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Reply to Zophar. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9507" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Job answered and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> No doubt but ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> the people, and wisdom shall die with you. <hi type="super">3</hi> But I have understanding as well as you; I <hi type="italic">am</hi> not inferior to you: yea, who knoweth not such things as these? <hi type="super">4</hi> I am <hi type="italic">as</hi> one mocked of his neighbour, who calleth upon God, and he answereth him: the just upright <hi type="italic">man is</hi> laughed to scorn. 5 He that is ready to slip with <hi type="italic">his</hi> feet <hi type="italic">is as</hi> a lamp despised in the thought of him that is at ease. <div eID="gen9507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9508" type="x-p"/> The reproofs Job here gives to his friends, whether they were just or no, were very sharp, and may serve for a rebuke to all that are proud and scornful, and an exposure of their folly. <div eID="gen9508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9509" type="x-p"/> I. He upbraids them with their conceitedness of themselves, and the good opinion they seemed to have of their own wisdom in comparison with him, than which nothing is more weak and unbecoming, nor better deserves to be ridiculed, as it is here. 1. He represents them as claiming the monopoly of wisdom, <reference osisRef="Job.12.2">v. 2</reference>. He speaks ironically: "<hi type="italic">No doubt you are the people;</hi> you think yourselves fit to dictate and give law to all mankind, and your own judgment to be the standard by which every man's opinion must be measured and tried, as if nobody could discern between truth and falsehood, good and evil, but you only; and therefore every top-sail must lower to you, and, right or wrong, we must all say as you say, and you three must be the people, the majority, to have the casting vote." Note, It is a very foolish and sinful thing for any to think themselves wiser than all mankind besides, or to speak and act confidently and imperiously, as if they thought so. Nay, he goes further: "You not only think there are none, but that there will be none, as wise as you, and therefore that <hi type="italic">wisdom must die with you,</hi> that all the world must be fools when you are gone, and in the dark when your sun has set." Note, It is folly for us to think that there will be any great irreparable loss of us when we are gone, or that we can be ill spared, since God has the residue of the Spirit, and can raise up others, more fit than we are, to do his work. When wise men and good men die it is a comfort to think that wisdom and goodness shall not die with them. Some think Job here reflects upon Zophar's comparing him (as he thought) and others to the wild ass's colt, <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">ch. xi. 12</reference>. "Yes," says he, "we must be asses; you are the only men." 2. He does himself the justice to put in his claim as a sharer in the gifts of wisdom (<reference osisRef="Job.12.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But I have understanding (a heart) as well as you;</hi> nay, <hi type="italic">I fall not lower than you;</hi>" as it is in the margin. "I am as well able to judge of the methods and meanings of the divine providence, and to construe the hard chapters of it, as you are." He says not this to magnify himself. It was no great applause of himself to say, <hi type="italic">I have understanding as well as you;</hi> no, nor to say, "I understand this matter as well as you;" for what reason had either he or they to be proud of understanding that which was obvious and level to the capacity of the meanest? "<hi type="italic">Yea, who knows not such things as these?</hi> What things you have said that are true are plain truths, and common themes, which there are many that can talk as excellently of as either you or I." But he says it to humble them, and check the value they had for themselves as doctors of the chair. Note, (1.) It may justly keep us from being proud of our knowledge to consider how many there are that know as much as we do, and perhaps much more and to better purpose. (2.) When we are tempted to be harsh in our censures of those we differ from and dispute with we ought to consider that they also have understanding as well as we, a capacity of judging, and a right of judging for themselves; nay, perhaps they are not inferior to us, but superior, and it is possible that they may be in the right and we in the wrong; and therefore we ought not to judge or despise them (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.3">Rom. xiv. 3</reference>), nor pretend to be masters (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.1">Jam. iii. 1</reference>), while <hi type="italic">all we are brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.8">Matt. xxiii. 8</reference>. It is a very reasonable allowance to be made to all we converse with, all we contend with, that they are rational creatures as well as we. <div eID="gen9509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9510" type="x-p"/> II. He complains of the great contempt with which they had treated him. Those that are haughty and think too well of themselves are commonly scornful and ready to trample upon all about them. Job found it so, at least he thought he did (<reference osisRef="Job.12.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am as one mocked.</hi> I cannot say there was cause for this charge; we will not think Job's friends designed him any abuse, nor aimed at any thing but to convince him, and so, in the right method, to comfort him; yet he cries out, <hi type="italic">I am as one mocked.</hi> Note, We are apt to call reproofs reproaches, and to think ourselves mocked when we are but advised and admonished; this peevishness is our folly, and a great wrong to ourselves and to our friends. Yet we cannot but say there was colour for this charge; they came to comfort him, but they vexed him, gave him counsels and encouragements, but with no great opinion that either the one or the other would take effect; and therefore he thought they mocked him, and this added much to his grief. Nothing is more grievous to those that have fallen from the height of prosperity into the depth of adversity than to be trodden on, and insulted over, when they are down; and on this head they are too apt to be suspicious. Observe, <div eID="gen9510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9511" type="x-p"/> 1. What aggravated this grievance to him. Two things:—(1.) That they were his <hi type="italic">neighbours,</hi> his friends, his companions (so the word signifies), and the scoffs of such are often most spitefully given, and always most indignantly received. <reference osisRef="Ps.55.12-Ps.55.13">Ps. lv. 12, 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">It was not an enemy that reproached me; then I would have</hi> slighted it, and <hi type="italic">so borne it; but it was thou, a man, my equal.</hi> (2.) That they were professors of religion, such as <hi type="italic">called upon God,</hi> and said that he <hi type="italic">answered them:</hi> for some understand that of the persons mocking. "They are such as have a regard to heaven, and an interest in heaven, whose prayers I would therefore be glad of and thankful for, whose good opinion I cannot but covet, and therefore whose censures are the more grievous." Note, It is sad that any who call upon God should mock their brethren (<reference osisRef="Jas.3.9-Jas.3.10">Jam. iii. 9, 10</reference>), and it cannot but lie heavily on a good man to be thought ill of by those whom he thinks well of, yet this is no new thing. <div eID="gen9511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9512" type="x-p"/> 2. What supported him under it. (1.) That he had a God to go to, with whom he could lodge his appeal; for some understand those words of the person mocked, that he <hi type="italic">calls upon God and he answers him;</hi> and so it agrees with <reference osisRef="Job.16.20">ch. xvi. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">My friends scorn me, but my eye poureth out tears to God.</hi> If our friends be deaf to our complaints, God is not; if they condemn us, God knows our integrity; if they make the worst of us, he will make the best of us; if they give us cross answers, he will give us kind ones. (2.) That his case was not singular, but very common: <hi type="italic">The just upright man is laughed to scorn.</hi> By many he is laughed at even for his justice and his uprightness, his honesty towards men and his piety towards God; these are derided as foolish things, which silly people needlessly hamper themselves with, as if religion were a jest and therefore to be made a jest of. By most he is laughed at for any little infirmity or weakness, notwithstanding his justice and uprightness, without any consideration had of that which is so much his honour. Note, It was of old the lot of honest good people to be despised and derided; we are not therefore to think it strange (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.12">1 Pet. iv. 12</reference>), no, nor to think it hard, if it be our lot; <hi type="italic">so persecuted they</hi> not only <hi type="italic">the prophets,</hi> but even the saints of the patriarchal age (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.12">Matt. v. 12</reference>), and can we expect to fare better than they? <div eID="gen9512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9513" type="x-p"/> 3. What he suspected to be the true cause of it, and that was, in short, this: they were themselves rich and at ease, and therefore they despised him who had fallen into poverty. It is the way of the world; we see instances of it daily. Those that prosper are praised, but of those that are going down it is said, "Down with them." <hi type="italic">He that is ready to slip with his feet</hi> and fall into trouble, though he has formerly shone as a lamp, is then looked upon as a lamp going out like the snuff of a candle, which we throw to the ground and tread upon, and is accordingly <hi type="italic">despised in the thought of him that is at ease,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.5">v. 5</reference>. Even the just upright man, that is in his generation as a burning and shining light, if he enter into temptation (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Ps. lxxiii. 2</reference>) or come under a cloud, is looked upon with contempt. See here, (1.) What is the common fault of those that live in prosperity. Being full, and easy, and merry themselves, they look scornfully upon those that are in want, pain, and sorrow; they overlook them, take no notice of them, and study to forget them. See <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Ps. cxxiii. 4</reference>. The chief butler drinks wine in bowls, but makes nothing of the afflictions of Joseph. Wealth without grace often makes men thus haughty, thus careless of their poor neighbours. (2.) What is the common fate of those that fall into adversity. Poverty serves to eclipse all their lustre; though they are lamps, yet, if taken out of golden candlesticks, and put, like Gideon's, into earthen pitchers, nobody values them as formerly, but those that live at ease despise them.
entries.fd7e15b520358e26d7fdeae45b487bc3ad4c03b2: <div eID="gen9513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9514" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> The tabernacles of robbers prosper, and they that provoke God are secure; into whose hand God bringeth <hi type="italic">abundantly.</hi> <hi type="super">7</hi> But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee; and the fowls of the air, and they shall tell thee: 8 Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach thee: and the fishes of the sea shall declare unto thee. <hi type="super">9</hi> Who knoweth not in all these that the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath wrought this? <hi type="super">10</hi> In whose hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> the soul of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind. <hi type="super">11</hi> Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth taste his meat? <div eID="gen9514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9515" type="x-p"/> Job's friends all of them went upon this principle, that wicked people cannot prosper long in this world, but some remarkable judgment or other will suddenly light on them: Zophar had concluded with it, that <hi type="italic">the eyes of the wicked shall fail,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.11.20">ch. xi. 20</reference>. This principle Job here opposes, and maintains that God, in disposing men's outward affairs, acts as a sovereign, reserving the exact distribution of rewards and punishments for the future state. <div eID="gen9515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9516" type="x-p"/> I. He asserts it as an undoubted truth that wicked people may, and often do, prosper long in this world, <reference osisRef="Job.12.6">v. 6</reference>. Even great sinners may enjoy great prosperity. Observe, 1. How he describes the sinners. They are <hi type="italic">robbers,</hi> and such as provoke God, the worst kind of sinners, blasphemers and persecutors. Perhaps he refers to the Sabeans and Chaldeans, who had robbed him, and had always lived by spoil and rapine, and yet they prospered; all the world saw they did, and there is no disputing against sense; one observation built upon matter of fact is worth twenty notions framed by an hypothesis. Or more generally, All proud oppressors are robbers and pirates. It is supposed that what is injurious to men is provoking to God, the patron of right and the protector of mankind. It is not strange if those that violate the bonds of justice break through the obligations of all religion, bid defiance even to God himself, and make nothing of provoking him. 2. How he describes their prosperity. It is very great; for, (1.) Even <hi type="italic">their tabernacles prosper,</hi> those that live with them and those that come after them and descend from them. It seems as if a blessing were entailed upon their families; and that is sometimes preserved to succeeding generations which was got by fraud. (2.) They <hi type="italic">are secure,</hi> and not only feel no hurt, but fear none, are under no apprehensions of danger either from threatening providences or an awakened conscience. But those <hi type="italic">that provoke God</hi> are never the more safe for their being secure. (3.) <hi type="italic">Into their hand God brings abundantly. They have more than heart could wish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Ps. lxxiii. 7</reference>), not for necessity only, but for delight—not for themselves only, but for others—not for the present only, but for hereafter; and this from the hand of Providence too. God brings plentifully to them. We cannot therefore judge of men's piety by their plenty, nor of what they have in their heart by what they have in their hand. <div eID="gen9516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9517" type="x-p"/> II. He appeals even to the inferior creatures for the proof of this—the beasts, and fowls, and trees, and even the earth itself; consult these, and they shall tell thee, <reference osisRef="Job.12.7-Job.12.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Many a good lesson we may learn from them, but what are they here to teach us? <div eID="gen9517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9518" type="x-p"/> 1. We may from them learn that <hi type="italic">the tabernacles of robbers prosper</hi> (so some); for, (1.) Even among the brute creatures the greater devour the less and the stronger prey upon the weaker, and men are as the fishes of the sea, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.14">Hab. i. 14</reference>. If sin had not entered, we may suppose there would have been no such disorder among the creatures, but the wolf and the lamb would have lain down together. (2.) These creatures are serviceable to wicked men, and so they declare their prosperity. Ask the herds and the flocks to whom they belong, and they will tell you that such a robber, such an oppressor, is their owner: the fishes and fowls will tell you that they are served up to the tables, and feed the luxury, of proud sinners. The earth brings forth her fruits to them (<reference osisRef="Job.9.24">ch. ix. 24</reference>), and the whole creation groans under the burden of their tyranny, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Rom. viii. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.22">22</reference>. Note, All the creatures which wicked men abuse, by making them the food and fuel of their lusts, will witness against them another day, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.3-Jas.5.4">Jam. v. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen9518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9519" type="x-p"/> 2. We may from them learn the wisdom, power, and goodness of God, and that sovereign dominion of his into which plain and self-evident truth all these difficult dispensations must be resolved. Zophar had made a vast mystery of it, <reference osisRef="Job.11.7">ch. xi. 7</reference>. "So far from that," says Job, "that what we are concerned to know we may learn even from the inferior creatures; for <hi type="italic">who knows not from all these?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.9">v. 9</reference>. Any one may easily gather from the book of the creatures that <hi type="italic">the hand of the Lord has wrought this,</hi>" that is, "that there is a wise Providence which guides and governs all these things by rules which we are neither acquainted with nor are competent judges of." Note, From God's sovereign dominion over the inferior creatures we should learn to acquiesce in all his disposals of the affairs of the children of men, though contrary to our measures. <div eID="gen9519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9520" type="x-p"/> III. He resolves all into the absolute propriety which God has in all the creatures (<reference osisRef="Job.12.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">In whose hand is the soul of every living thing.</hi> All the creatures, and mankind particularly, derive their being from him, owe their being to him, depend upon him for the support of it, lie at his mercy, are under his direction and dominion and entirely at his disposal, and at his summons must resign their lives. All souls are his; and may he not do what he will with his own? The name <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> is used here (<reference osisRef="Job.12.9">v. 9</reference>), and it is the only time that we meet with it in all the discourses between Job and his friends; for God was, in that age, more known by the name of <hi type="italic">Shaddai—the Almighty.</hi> <div eID="gen9520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9521" type="x-p"/> IV. Those words—(<reference osisRef="Job.12.11">v. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Doth not the ear try words, as the mouth tastes meat?</hi> may be taken either as the conclusion to the foregoing discourse or the preface to what follows. The mind of man has as good a faculty of discerning between truth and error, when duly stated, as the palate has of discerning between what is sweet and what is bitter. Job therefore demands from his friends a liberty to judge for himself of what they had said, and desires them to use the same liberty in judging of what he had said; nay, he seems to appeal to any man's impartial judgment in this controversy; let the ear try the words on both sides, and it would be found that he was in the right. Note, The ear must try words before it receives them so as to subscribe to them. As by the taste we judge what food is wholesome to the body and what not, so by the spirit of discerning we must judge what doctrine is sound, and savoury, and wholesome, and what not, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.15">1 Cor. x. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.13">xi. 13</reference>.
entries.f7d38aba5e4818ba8be5047e6bf235d6f1c3d904: <div eID="gen9521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9522" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> With the ancient <hi type="italic">is</hi> wisdom; and in length of days understanding. <hi type="super">13</hi> With him <hi type="italic">is</hi> wisdom and strength, he hath counsel and understanding. <hi type="super">14</hi> Behold, he breaketh down, and it cannot be built again: he shutteth up a man, and there can be no opening. <hi type="super">15</hi> Behold, he withholdeth the waters, and they dry up: also he sendeth them out, and they overturn the earth. <hi type="super">16</hi> With him <hi type="italic">is</hi> strength and wisdom: the deceived and the deceiver <hi type="italic">are</hi> his. <hi type="super">17</hi> He leadeth counsellors away spoiled, and maketh the judges fools. 18 He looseth the bond of kings, and girdeth their loins with a girdle. <hi type="super">19</hi> He leadeth princes away spoiled, and overthroweth the mighty. <hi type="super">20</hi> He removeth away the speech of the trusty, and taketh away the understanding of the aged. <hi type="super">21</hi> He poureth contempt upon princes, and weakeneth the strength of the mighty. <hi type="super">22</hi> He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth out to light the shadow of death. <hi type="super">23</hi> He increaseth the nations, and destroyeth them: he enlargeth the nations, and straiteneth them <hi type="italic">again.</hi> <hi type="super">24</hi> He taketh away the heart of the chief of the people of the earth, and causeth them to wander in a wilderness <hi type="italic">where there is</hi> no way. <hi type="super">25</hi> They grope in the dark without light, and he maketh them to stagger like <hi type="italic">a</hi> drunken <hi type="italic">man.</hi> <div eID="gen9522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9523" type="x-p"/> This is a noble discourse of Job's concerning the wisdom, power, and sovereignty of God, in ordering and disposing of all the affairs of the children of men, according to the counsel of his own will, which none dares gainsay or can resist. Take both him and them out of the controversy in which they were so warmly engaged, and they all spoke admirably well; but, in <hi type="italic">that,</hi> we sometimes scarcely know what to make of them. It were well if wise and good men, that differ in their apprehensions about minor things, would see it to be for their honour and comfort, and the edification of others, to dwell most upon those great things in which they are agreed. On this subject Job speaks like himself. Here are no passionate complaints, no peevish reflections, but every thing masculine and great. <div eID="gen9523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9524" type="x-p"/> I. He asserts the unsearchable wisdom and irresistible power of God. It is allowed that among men there is <hi type="italic">wisdom and understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.12">v. 12</reference>. But it is to be found only with some few, <hi type="italic">with the ancient,</hi> and those who are blessed with length of days, who get it by long experience and constant experience; and, when they have got the wisdom, they have lost their strength and are unable to execute the results of their wisdom. But now <hi type="italic">with God there are</hi> both <hi type="italic">wisdom and strength,</hi> wisdom to design the best and strength to accomplish what is designed. He does not get counsel or understanding, as we do, by observation, but he has it essentially and eternally in himself, <reference osisRef="Job.12.13">v. 13</reference>. What is the wisdom of ancient men compared with the wisdom of the ancient of days! It is but little that we know, and less that we can do; but God can do every thing, and <hi type="italic">no thought can be withheld from him.</hi> Happy are those who have this God for their God, for they have infinite wisdom and strength engaged for them. Foolish and fruitless are all the attempts of men against him (<reference osisRef="Job.12.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">He breaketh down, and it cannot be built again.</hi> Note, There is no contending with the divine providence, nor breaking the measures of it. As he had said before (<reference osisRef="Job.9.12">ch. ix. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">He takes away, and who can hinder him?</hi> so he says again. What God says cannot be gainsaid, nor what he does undone. There is no rebuilding what God will have to lie in ruins; witness the tower of Babel, which the undertakers could not go on with, and the desolations of Sodom and Gomorrah, which could never be repaired. See <reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa. xxv. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.14">Ezek. xxvi. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.21">Rev. xviii. 21</reference>. There is no releasing those whom God has condemned to a perpetual imprisonment; if <hi type="italic">he shut up</hi> a man by sickness, reduce him to straits, and embarrass him in his affairs, <hi type="italic">there can be no opening.</hi> He shuts up in the grave, and none can break open those sealed doors—shuts up in hell, in chains of darkness, and none can pass that great gulf fixed. <div eID="gen9524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9525" type="x-p"/> II. He gives an instance, for the proof of this doctrine in nature, <reference osisRef="Job.12.15">v. 15</reference>. God has the command of <hi type="italic">the waters, binds them as in a garment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.30.4">Prov. xxx. 4</reference>), holds them <hi type="italic">in the hollow of his hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Isa. xl. 12</reference>); and he can punish the children of men either by the defect or by the excess of them. As men break the laws of virtue by extremes on each hand, both defects and excesses, while virtue is in the mean, so God corrects them by extremes, and denies them the mercy which is in the mean. 1. Great droughts are sometimes great judgments: <hi type="italic">He withholds the waters, and they dry up;</hi> if the heaven be as brass, the earth is as iron; if the rain be denied, fountains dry up and their streams are wanted, fields are parched and their fruits are wanted, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.7">Amos iv. 7</reference>. 2. Great wet is sometimes a great judgment. He raises the waters, and <hi type="italic">overturns the earth,</hi> the productions of it, the buildings upon it. A sweeping rain is said to <hi type="italic">leave no food,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.3">Prov. xxviii. 3</reference>. See how many ways God has of contending with a sinful people and taking from them abused, forfeited, mercies; and how utterly unable we are to contend with him. If we might invert the order, <reference osisRef="Job.12.15">this verse</reference> would fitly refer to Noah's flood, that ever memorable instance of the divine power. God then, in wrath, sent the waters out, and they overturned the earth; but in mercy he withheld them, shut the windows of heaven and the fountains of the great deep, and then, in a little time, they dried up. <div eID="gen9525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9526" type="x-p"/> III. He gives many instances of it in God's powerful management of the children of men, crossing their purposes and serving his own by them and upon them, overruling all their counsels, overpowering all their attempts, and overcoming all their oppositions. What changes does God make with men! what turns does he give them! how easily, how surprisingly! <div eID="gen9526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9527" type="x-p"/> 1. In general (<reference osisRef="Job.12.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">With him are strength and reason</hi> (so some translate it), strength and consistency with himself: it is an elegant word in the original. With him are the very quintessence and extract of wisdom. <hi type="italic">With him are power and all that is;</hi> so some read it. He is what he is of himself, and by him and in him all things subsist. Having this strength and wisdom, he knows how to make use, not only of those who are wise and good, who willingly and designedly serve him, but even of those who are foolish and bad, who, one would think, could be made no way serviceable to the designs of his providence: <hi type="italic">The deceived and the deceiver are his;</hi> the simplest men that are deceived are not below his notice; the subtlest men that deceive cannot with all their subtlety escape his cognizance. The world is full of deceit; the one half of mankind cheats the other, and God suffers it to be so, and from both will at last bring glory to himself. The deceivers make tools of the deceived, but the great God makes tools of them both, wherewith he works, and none can hinder him. He has wisdom and might enough to manage all the fools and knaves in the world, and knows how to serve his own purposes by them, notwithstanding the weakness of the one and the wickedness of the other. When Jacob by a fraud got the blessing the design of God's grace was served; when Ahab was drawn by a false prophecy into an expedition that was his ruin the design of God's justice was served; and in both <hi type="italic">the deceived and the deceiver</hi> were at his disposal. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.9">Ezek. xiv. 9</reference>. God would not suffer the sin of the deceiver, nor the misery of the deceived, if he knew not how to set bounds to both and bring glory to himself out of both. <hi type="italic">Hallelujah, the Lord God omnipotent</hi> thus reigns; and it is well he does, for otherwise there is so little wisdom and so little honesty in the world that it would all have been in confusion and ruin long ago. <div eID="gen9527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9528" type="x-p"/> 2. He next descends to the particular instances of the wisdom and power of God in the revolutions of states and kingdoms; for thence he fetches his proofs, rather than from the like operations of Providence concerning private persons and families, because the more high and public the station is in which men are placed the more the changes that befal them are taken notice of, and consequently the more illustriously does Providence shine forth in them. And it is easy to argue, If God can thus turn and toss the great ones of the earth, like a ball in a large place (as the prophet speaks, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Isa. xxii. 18</reference>), much more the little ones; and with him to whom states and kingdoms must submit it is surely the greatest madness for us to contend. Some think that Job here refers to the extirpation of those powerful nations, the Rephaim, the Zuzim, the Emim, and the Horites (mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.14.5-Gen.14.6">Gen. xiv. 5, 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.10 Deut.2.20">Deut. ii. 10, 20</reference>), in which perhaps it was particularly noticed how strangely they were infatuated and enfeebled: if so, it is designed to show that whenever the like is done in the affairs of nations it is God that does it, and we must therein observe his sovereign dominion, even over those that think themselves most powerful, politic, and absolute. Compare this with that of Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.5.12-Job.5.14">ch. v. 12</reference>, &c. Let us gather up the particular changes here specified, which God makes upon persons, either for the destruction of nations and the planting of others in their room or for the turning out of a particular government and ministry and the elevation of another in its room, which may be a blessing to the kingdom; witness the glorious Revolution in our own land twenty years ago, in which we saw as happy an exposition as ever was given of this discourse of Job's. (1.) Those that were wise are sometimes strangely infatuated, and in this the hand of God must be acknowledged (<reference osisRef="Job.12.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">He leadeth counsellors away spoiled,</hi> as trophies of his victory over them, spoiled of all the honour and wealth they have got by their policy, nay, spoiled of the wisdom itself for which they have been celebrated and the success they promised themselves in their projects. His counsel stands, while all their devices are brought to nought and their designs baffled, and so they are spoiled both of the satisfaction and of the reputation of their wisdom. <hi type="italic">He maketh the judges fools.</hi> By a work on their minds he deprives them of their qualifications for business, and so they become really fools; and by his disposal of their affairs he makes the issue and event of their projects to be quite contrary to what they themselves intended, and so he makes them look like fools. The counsel of Ahithophel, one in whom this scripture was remarkably fulfilled, became foolishness, and he, according to his name, <hi type="italic">the brother of a fool.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.19.13">Isa. xix. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">The princes of Zoan have become fools; they have seduced Egypt, even those that are the stay of the tribes thereof.</hi> Let not the wise man therefore glory in his wisdom, nor the ablest counsellors and judges be proud of their station, but humbly depend upon God for the continuance of their abilities. Even the aged, who seem to hold their wisdom by prescription, and think they have got it by their own industry and therefore have an indefeasible title to it, may yet be deprived of it, and often are, by the infirmities of age, which make them twice children: He <hi type="italic">taketh away the understanding of the aged,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.20">v. 20</reference>. The aged, who were most depended on for advice, fail those that depended on them. We read of an old and yet foolish king, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13">Eccl. iv. 13</reference>. (2.) Those that were high and in authority are strangely brought down, impoverished, and enslaved, and it is God that humbles them (<reference osisRef="Job.12.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">He looseth the bond of kings,</hi> and taketh from them the power wherewith they ruled their subjects, perhaps enslaved them and ruled them with rigour; he strips them of all the ensigns of their honour and authority, and all the supports of their tyranny, unbuckles their belts, so that the sword drops from their side, and then no marvel if the crown quickly drops from their head, on which immediately follows the <hi type="italic">girding of their loins with a girdle,</hi> a badge of servitude, for servants went with their loins girt. Thus <hi type="italic">he leads</hi> great <hi type="italic">princes away spoiled</hi> of all their power and wealth, and that in which they pleased and prided themselves, <reference osisRef="Job.12.19">v. 19</reference>. Note, Kings are not exempt from God's jurisdiction. To us they are gods, but men to him, and subject to more than the common changes of human life. (3.) Those that were strong are strangely weakened, and it is God that weakens them (<reference osisRef="Job.12.21">v. 21</reference>) and <hi type="italic">overthrows the mighty.</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.12.19">v. 19</reference>. Strong bodies are weakened by age and sickness; powerful armies moulder and come to nothing, and their strength will not secure them from a fatal overthrow. No force can stand before Omnipotence, no, not that of Goliath. (4.) Those that were famed for eloquence, and entrusted with public business, are strangely silenced, and have nothing to say (<reference osisRef="Job.12.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">He removeth away the speech of the trusty,</hi> so that they cannot speak as they intended and as they used to do, with freedom and clearness, but blunder, and falter, and make nothing of it. Or they cannot speak what they intended, but the contrary, as Balaam, who blessed those whom he was called to curse. Let not the orator therefore be proud of his rhetoric, nor use it to any bad purposes, lest God take it away, who made man's mouth. (5.) Those that were honoured and admired strangely fall into disgrace (<reference osisRef="Job.12.21">v. 21</reference>): He <hi type="italic">poureth contempt upon princes.</hi> He leaves them to themselves to do mean things, or alters the opinions of men concerning them. If princes themselves dishonour God and despise him, if they offer indignities to the people of God and trample upon them, they shall be lightly esteemed, and God will pour contempt upon them. See <reference osisRef="Ps.107.40">Ps. cvii. 40</reference>. Commonly none more abject in themselves, nor more abused by others when they are down, than those who were haughty and insolent when they were in power. (6.) That which was secret, and lay hidden, is strangely brought to light and laid open (<reference osisRef="Job.12.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">He discovers deep things out of darkness.</hi> Plots closely laid are discovered and defeated; wickedness closely committed and artfully concealed is discovered, and the guilty are brought to condign punishment—secret treasons (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.20">Eccl. x. 20</reference>), secret murders, secret whoredoms. The cabinet-councils of princes are before God's eye, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.11">2 Kings vi. 11</reference>. (7.) Kingdoms have their ebbings and flowings, their waxings and wanings; and both are from God (<reference osisRef="Job.12.23">v. 23</reference>): He sometimes <hi type="italic">increases their numbers,</hi> and enlarges their bounds, so that they make a figure among the nations and become formidable; but after a while, by some undiscerned cause perhaps, they are destroyed and straitened, made few and poor, cut short and many of them cut off, and so they are rendered despicable among their neighbours, and those that were the head become the tail of the nations. See <reference osisRef="Ps.107.38-Ps.107.39">Ps. cvii. 38, 39</reference>. (8.) Those that were bold and courageous, and made nothing of dangers, are strangely cowed and dispirited; and this also is the Lord's doing (<reference osisRef="Job.12.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">He taketh away the heart of the chief of the people,</hi> that were their leaders and commanders, and were most famed for their martial fire and great achievements; when any thing is to be done they are heartless, and ready to flee at the shaking of a leaf. <reference osisRef="Ps.76.5">Ps. lxvi. 5</reference>. (9.) Those that were driving on their projects with full speed are strangely bewildered and at a loss; they know not where they are nor what they do, are unsteady in their counsels and uncertain in their motions, off and on, this way and that way, wandering like men in a desert (<reference osisRef="Job.12.24">v. 24</reference>), groping like men in the dark, and staggering like men in drink, <reference osisRef="Job.12.25">v. 25.</reference> <reference osisRef="Isa.59.10">Isa. lix. 10</reference>. Note, God can soon nonplus the deepest politicians and bring the greatest wits to their wits' end, to show that wherein they deal proudly he is above them. <div eID="gen9528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9529" type="x-p"/> Thus are the revolutions of kingdoms wonderfully brought about by an overruling Providence. Heaven and earth are shaken, but the Lord sits King for ever, and with him we look for <hi type="italic">a kingdom that cannot be shaken.</hi>  <chapter eID="Job.12"/> <div eID="gen9529" type="x-p"/>

entries.9a3830947d993b51ff89c233ceb884f2ce4b69c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4687"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <div sID="gen6805" type="x-p"/> FIRST SERIES.<div eID="gen6805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6806" type="x-p"/> Job 12:<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.22">1-14:22</reference>. Job's Reply to Zophar<div eID="gen6806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6807" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4687"/><hi type="bold">2. wisdom shall die with you--</hi>Ironical, as if all the wisdom in the world was concentrated in them and would expire when they expired. Wisdom makes "a people:" a foolish nation is "not a people" (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.19">Ro 10:19</reference>). <div eID="gen6807" type="x-p"/>
entries.48f0edc2322d3356a89992e91cb722b1903bd6b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4688"/><div sID="gen6808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4688"/><hi type="bold">3. not inferior--</hi>not vanquished in argument and "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Job.13.2">Job 13:2</reference>).<div eID="gen6808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">such things as these--</hi>such commonplace maxims as you so pompously adduce. <div eID="gen6809" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b6903b347dca008c5f063c4b6f9a7fe60d7f836: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4689"/><div sID="gen6810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4689"/>4. The unfounded accusations of Job's friends were a "mockery" of him. He alludes to Zophar's word, "mockest" (<reference osisRef="Job.11.3">Job 11:3</reference>).<div eID="gen6810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neighbour, who calleth, &c.--</hi>rather, "I who call upon God that he may answer me favorably" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6811" type="x-p"/>
entries.e02f3bfeecec3e6cde373b923543831b7f4eb788: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4690"/><div sID="gen6812" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4690"/>5. Rather, "a torch" (lamp) is an object of contempt in the thoughts of him who rests securely (is at ease), though it was prepared for the falterings of the feet [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.19">Pr 25:19</reference>). "Thoughts" and "feet" are in contrast; also rests "securely," and "falterings." The wanderer, arrived at his night-quarters, contemptuously throws aside the torch which had guided his uncertain steps through the darkness. As the torch is to the wanderer, so Job to his friends. Once they gladly used his aid in their need; now they in prosperity mock him in his need. <div eID="gen6812" type="x-p"/>
entries.cde1d90e7227719324a3476d89b917020104bdf9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4691"/><div sID="gen6813" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4691"/>6. Job shows that the matter of fact opposes Zophar's theory (<reference osisRef="Job.11.14">Job 11:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.20">19, 20</reference>) that wickedness causes insecurity in men's "tabernacles." On the contrary, they who rob the "tabernacles" ("dwellings") of others "prosper securely" in their own.<div eID="gen6813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into whose hand, &c.--</hi>rather, "who make a god of their own hand," that is, who regard their might as their only ruling principle [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6814" type="x-p"/>
entries.d78b66b4eeedbee2449ac3fa34ce37570c8aa92d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4692"/><div sID="gen6815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4692"/>7-8. Beasts, birds, fishes, and plants, reasons Job, teach that the violent live the most securely (<reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference>). The vulture lives more securely than the dove, the lion than the ox, the shark than the dolphin, the rose than the thorn which tears it. <div eID="gen6815" type="x-p"/>
entries.263d939d100898debf473d5f6fc50c9522474c1d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4694"/><div sID="gen6817" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4694"/>9. In all these cases, says Job, the agency must be referred to Jehovah, though they may seem to man to imply imperfection (<reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.24">9:24</reference>). This is the only undisputed passage of the poetical part in which the name "Jehovah" occurs; in the historical parts it occurs frequently. <div eID="gen6817" type="x-p"/>
entries.093d44e8ed63bac459ee869c4e24a6870b683385: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4695"/><div sID="gen6818" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4695"/><hi type="bold">10. the soul--</hi>that is, the animal life. Man, reasons Job, is subjected to the same laws as the lower animals. <div eID="gen6818" type="x-p"/>
entries.a23b285a46576fafe379f48857ed7f2b6bd1189a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4696"/><div sID="gen6819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4696"/>11. As the mouth by tasting meats selects what pleases it, so the ear tries the words of others and retains what is convincing. Each chooses according to his taste. The connection with <reference osisRef="Job.12.12">Job 12:12</reference> is in reference to Bildad's appeal to the "ancients" (<reference osisRef="Job.8.8">Job 8:8</reference>). You are right in appealing to them, since "with them was wisdom," &c. But you select such proverbs of theirs as suit your views; so I may borrow from the same such as suit mine. <div eID="gen6819" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc90c44ecc2410352312139612617861a4224095: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4697"/><div sID="gen6820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4697"/><hi type="bold">12. ancient--</hi>aged (<reference osisRef="Job.15.10">Job 15:10</reference>). <div eID="gen6820" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5eb52a2e35ee036599ae9a16bbc0ef559521908: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4698"/><div sID="gen6821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4698"/>13. In contrast to, "with the ancient is wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Job.12.12">Job 12:12</reference>), Job quotes a saying of the ancients which suits his argument, "with Him (God) is (the true) wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.14">Pr 8:14</reference>); and by that "wisdom and strength" "He breaketh down," &c., as an absolute Sovereign, not allowing man to penetrate His mysteries; man's part is to bow to His unchangeable decrees (<reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference>). The Mohammedan saying is, "if God will, and how God will." <div eID="gen6821" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0221e8b04a76135535ebee49bdc5fa193597837: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4699"/><div sID="gen6822" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4699"/><hi type="bold">14. shutteth up--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">Is 22:22</reference>). Job refers to Zophar's "shut up" (<reference osisRef="Job.11.10">Job 11:10</reference>). <div eID="gen6822" type="x-p"/>
entries.49bfa40c30957b1ce1af8b0080b212df8ec2af9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4700"/><div sID="gen6823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4700"/>15. Probably alluding to the flood. <div eID="gen6823" type="x-p"/>
entries.158233a4f87b7874bc45da7b128795f54ab951b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4701"/><div sID="gen6824" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4701"/>16. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.14.9">Eze 14:9</reference>). <div eID="gen6824" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0628f97cc4fd9b53a606e85fcf09e0ed0bd8725: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4702"/><div sID="gen6825" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4702"/><hi type="bold">18. He looseth the bond of kings--</hi>He looseth the authority of kings--the "bond" with which they bind their subjects (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">Is 45:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.14.4">Ge 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.21">Da 2:21</reference>).<div eID="gen6825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a girdle--</hi>the cord, with which they are bound as captives, instead of the royal "girdle" they once wore (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.21">Is 22:21</reference>), and the bond they once bound others with. So "gird"--put on one the bonds of a prisoner instead of the ordinary girdle (<reference osisRef="John.21.18">Joh 21:18</reference>). <div eID="gen6826" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7c660850533fb6fd58243014cbb9278a59ac491: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4703"/><div sID="gen6827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4703"/><hi type="bold">19. princes--</hi>rather, "priests," as the Hebrew is rendered (<reference osisRef="Ps.99.6">Psa 99:6</reference>). Even the sacred ministers of religion are not exempt from reverses and captivity.<div eID="gen6827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mighty--</hi>rather, "the firm-rooted in power"; the Arabic root expresses ever-flowing water [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6828" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a50a927094b91a2e55d00c8a7845732cbfb921f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4704"/><div sID="gen6829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4704"/><hi type="bold">20. the trusty--</hi>rather, "those secure in their eloquence"; for example, the speakers in the gate (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.3">Is 3:3</reference>) [Beza].<div eID="gen6829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">understanding--</hi>literally, "taste," that is, insight or spiritual discernment, which experience gives the aged. The same Hebrew word is applied to Daniel's wisdom in interpretation (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.14">Da 2:14</reference>). <div eID="gen6830" type="x-p"/>
entries.2aaee1e733450446b8bb8243d855f788f5e96244: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4705"/><div sID="gen6831" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4705"/>21. <reference osisRef="Ps.107.40">Psa 107:40</reference> quotes, in its first clause, this verse and, in its second, <reference osisRef="Job.12.24">Job 12:24</reference>.<div eID="gen6831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weakeneth the strength--</hi>literally, "looseth the girdle"; Orientals wear flowing garments; when active strength is to be put forth, they gird up their garments with a girdle. Hence here--"He destroyeth their power" in the eyes of the people. <div eID="gen6832" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b7dc999ac3cd789008f7ee0d7ae478fb1baf461: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4706"/><div sID="gen6833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4706"/>22. (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.22">Da 2:22</reference>). <div eID="gen6833" type="x-p"/>
entries.3027078cf553f9ed98964d83b1025fb639972e47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4707"/><div sID="gen6834" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4707"/>23. <reference osisRef="Isa.9.3">Is 9:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.38">Psa 107:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.39">39</reference>, which Psalm quotes this chapter elsewhere. (See on <reference osisRef="Job.12.21">Job 12:21</reference>).<div eID="gen6834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">straiteneth--</hi>literally, "leadeth in," that is, "reduces." <div eID="gen6835" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed3817c0090d08f3397170c31be824b75f1d5c89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4708"/><div sID="gen6836" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4708"/><hi type="bold">24. heart--</hi>intelligence.<div eID="gen6836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wander in a wilderness--</hi>figurative; not referring to any actual fact. This cannot be quoted to prove Job lived after Israel's wanderings in the desert. <reference osisRef="Ps.107.4">Psa 107:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.40">40</reference> quotes this passage. <div eID="gen6837" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb9b38f3e8f5c0f483853ed827265aad46df7f0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4709"/><div sID="gen6838" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4709"/>25. <reference osisRef="Deut.28.29">De 28:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.27">Psa 107:27</reference> again quote Job, but in a different connection. <chapter eID="Job.12"/>

entries.6b9bc14ed68abad722f301f782f07f9bd2b14560: <div eID="gen16367" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16368" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16369" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16369" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16368" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16370" type="x-p"/> Job reproves the boasting of his friends, and shows their uncharitableness towards himself, <reference osisRef="Job.12.1-Job.12.5">Job 12:1-5</reference>; asserts that even the tabernacles of robbers prosper; and that, notwithstanding, God is the Governor of the world; a truth which is proclaimed by all parts of the creation whether animate or inanimate, and by the revolutions which take place in states, vv. 6-25.
entries.8a23bc1346ddd67c23065f5fb62467a68bb825c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16371" type="x-p"/> No doubt but ye are the people - Doubtless ye are the wisest men in the world; all wisdom is concentrated in you; and when ye die, there will no more be found on the face of the earth! This is a strong irony.
entries.87a7e1b2e0a132a5b940a4d17ffda8be5c424df2: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16372" type="x-p"/> I am not inferior to you - I do not fall short of any of you in understanding, wisdom, learning, and experience. <div eID="gen16372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16373" type="x-p"/> Who knoweth not such things as these? - All your boasted wisdom consists only in strings of proverbs which are in every person's mouth, and are no proof of wisdom and experience in them that use them.
entries.3e2e894a073017beb407dc84cd154423c83c1bd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16374" type="x-p"/> I am as one mocked of his neighbor - Though I am invoking God for help and salvation, yet my friends mock me in this most solemn and sacred work. But God answereth me. <div eID="gen16374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16375" type="x-p"/> The just upright man is laughed to scorn - This is a very difficult verse, on which no two critics seem to be agreed. Mr. Good translates the fourth and fifth verses thus: - "Thus brother is become a laughing-stock to his companions, <div eID="gen16375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16376" type="x-p"/> While calling upon God that he would succor him. <div eID="gen16376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16377" type="x-p"/> The just, the perfect man, is a laughing-stock to the proud, <div eID="gen16377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16378" type="x-p"/> A derision amidst the sunshine of the prosperous, <div eID="gen16378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16379" type="x-p"/> While ready to slip with his foot. <div eID="gen16379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16380" type="x-p"/> For a vindication of this version, I must refer to his notes. Coverdale gives at least a good sense. Thus he that calleth upon God, and whom God heareth, is mocked of his neighboure: the godly and innocent man is laughed to scorne. Godlynesse is a light despysed in the hertes of the rich; and is set for them to stomble upon. The fifth verse is thus rendered by Mr. Parkhurst: "A torch of contempt, or contemptible link, (see <reference osisRef="Isa.7.4">Isa 7:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Isa 40:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference>), לעשתות leashtoth, to the splendours of the prosperous (is he who is) ready (נכון nachon, <reference osisRef="Job.15.23">Job 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.38.17">Psa 38:17</reference>) to slip with his foot." The general sense is tolerably plain; but to emendations and conjectures there is no end.
entries.3f155dfa74ea83ef3c72b884b6e17370c2ac16a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16381" type="x-p"/> The tabernacles of robbers prosper - Those who live by the plunder of their neighbors are often found in great secular prosperity; and they that provoke God by impiety and blasphemy live in a state of security and affluence. These are administrations of Providence which cannot be accounted for; yet the Judge of all the earth does right. Therefore prosperity and adversity are no evidences of a man's spiritual state, nor of the place he holds in the approbation or disapprobation of God.
entries.d23149e72e5ca82d3f6e3d0be72acf1ab0412183: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16382" type="x-p"/> But ask now the beasts, and they shall teach thee - Mr. Good's paraphrase here is very just: "Why tell ye me that the Almighty hath brought this calamity upon me? Every thing in nature, the beasts of the field, the fowls of the heaven, every inhabitant of earth and sea, and every thing that befalls them, are the work of his hands; and every thing feels and acknowledges him to be the universal Creator and Controller. It is the common doctrine of all nature; but to apply it as ye would apply it to me, and to assert that I am suffering from being guilty of hypocrisy, is equally impertinent. He ordains every thing in wisdom as well as in power; but why events happen as they happen, why good and evil are promiscuously scattered throughout nature or human life, ye are as ignorant of as myself."
entries.bf9bea3e2460671586e0dc86c066270d3f113781: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16383" type="x-p"/> In whose hand is the soul of every living thing - נפש כל חי nephesh col chai, "the soul of all life." <div eID="gen16383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16384" type="x-p"/> And the breath of all mankind - ורוח כל בשר veruach col besar, "and the spirit or breath of all flesh." Does not the first refer to the immortal soul, the principle of all intellectual life; and the latter to the breath, respiration, the grand means by which animal existence is continued? See <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">Job 10:1</reference>.
entries.5ef1d6b9c33e063f9676ea9b00b2ad7b7d8eb496: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16385" type="x-p"/> Doth not the ear try words? - All these are common-place sayings. Ye have advanced nothing new; ye have cast no light upon the dispensations of Providence.
entries.e308e830d0bf0cbad5fc92d9ef9631327701249a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16386" type="x-p"/> With the ancient is wisdom - Men who have lived in those primitive times, when the great facts of nature were recent, such as the creation, fall, flood, confusion of tongues, migration of families, and consequent settlement of nations, had much knowledge from those facts; and their length of days - the many hundreds of years to which they lived, gave them such an opportunity of accumulating wisdom by experience, that they are deservedly considered as oracles.
entries.8273a1120cffef4a3a98ef9fe19e5335ecf48286: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16387" type="x-p"/> With him is wisdom and strength - But all these things come from God; he is the Fountain of wisdom and the Source of power. He alone can give us unerring counsel, and understanding to comprehend and act profitably by it. See on <reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job 12:16</reference> (note).
entries.3903fc945073ff507db9b21cda786f28432a2d4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16388" type="x-p"/> He breaketh down - He alone can create, and he alone can destroy. Nothing can be annihilated but by the same Power that created it. This is a most remarkable fact. No power, skill, or cunning of man can annihilate the smallest particle of matter. Man, by chemical agency, may change its form; but to reduce it to nothing belongs to God alone. In the course of his providence God breaks down, so that it cannot be built up again. See proofs of this in the total political destruction of Nineveh, Babylon, Persepolis, Tyre, and other cities, which have broken down never to be rebuilt; as well as the Assyrian, Babylonian, Grecian, and Roman empires, which have been dismembered and almost annihilated, never more to be regenerated. <div eID="gen16388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16389" type="x-p"/> He shutteth up a man - He often frustrates the best laid purposes, so that they can never be brought to good effect.
entries.9fe05c732eaefeb0760e881d43da6a9a07f19e76: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16390" type="x-p"/> He withholdeth the waters - This is, I think, an allusion to the third day's work of the creation, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.9">Gen 1:9</reference> : And God said, Let the waters be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear. Thus the earth was drained, and the waters collected into seas, and bound to their particular places. <div eID="gen16390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16391" type="x-p"/> Also he sendeth them out - Here is also an allusion to the flood, for when he broke up the fountains of the great deep, then the earth was overturned.
entries.ac1305c748c4bb81432372073353a763477cd378: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16392" type="x-p"/> With him is strength and wisdom - עז ותושיה oz vethushiyah, strength and sufficiency. Strength or power, springing from an exhaustless and infinite source of potency. In the thirteenth verse it is said, With him is wisdom and strength; but the expressions are not the same, חכמה וגבורה chochmah ugeburah, intelligence and fortitude, or strength in action, the wisdom ever guiding the exertions of power; but here is strength or power in essence, and an eternal potentiality. With him is every excellence, in potentia and in esse. He borrows nothing, he derives nothing. As he is self-existent, so is he self-sufficient. We have had the word tushiyah before. See the note on <reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job 11:6</reference>. <div eID="gen16392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16393" type="x-p"/> The deceived and the deceiver are his - Some think this refers to the fall; even Satan the deceiver or beguiler, and Adam and Eve, the deceived or beguiled, are his. Satan, as this book shows, cannot act without especial permission; and man, whom the seducer thought to make his own property for ever, is claimed as the peculium or especial property of God, for the seed of the woman was then appointed to bruise the head of the serpent; and Jesus Christ has assumed the nature of man, and thus brought human nature into a state of fellowship with himself. Thus he who sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one, for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.11">Heb 2:11</reference>.
entries.caa4377fbdf94f60e90e7de2fcdcc0e29a4bd86d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16394" type="x-p"/> He leadeth counsellors away spoiled - The events of war are also in his hand. It is he who gives victory; through him even the counsellors - the great men and chief men, are often led into captivity, and found among the spoils. <div eID="gen16394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16395" type="x-p"/> And maketh the judges fools - He infatuates the judges. Does this refer to the foolish conduct of some of the Israelitish judges, such as Samson?
entries.73c7648ad20d9f746331b5ba346aa45017e2dbd9: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16396" type="x-p"/> He looseth the bond of kings - He takes away their splendid robes, and clothes them with sackcloth; or, he dissolves their authority, permits their subjects to rebel and overthrow the state, to bind them as captives, and despoil them of all power, authority, and liberty. Many proofs of this occur in the Israelitish history and in the history of the principal nations of the earth, and not a few in the history of Britain.
entries.0df6de111064f879f59d97a0eea77f3eec79abb0: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16397" type="x-p"/> He leadeth princes away spoiled, and overthroweth the mighty - What multitudes of proofs of this does the history of the world present! Even the late disastrous war with the French republic and empire, which began in 1793, and continued without intermission till 1814, was afterwards renewed, and had a catastrophe that went nearly to ruin Europe. How many princes, or rather priests, כהנים cohanim, have been spoiled of their power, influence, and authority; and how many mighty men - captains, generals, admirals, etc., have been overthrown! But supposing that the writer of the Book of Job lived, as some think, after the captivity, how many priests were led away spoiled, both from Israel and Judah; and how many kings and mighty men were overthrown in the disastrous wars between the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Jews!
entries.8ea66f2aec007e904fbc38f1772bbd7ac968da99: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16398" type="x-p"/> He removeth away the speech of the trusty - The faithful counsellor and the eloquent orator avail nothing: Quos Deus vult perdere, prius dementat; "God infatuates those whom he is determined to destroy." The writer might have had his eyes on <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1-Isa.3.3">Isa 3:1-3</reference>, which the reader will do well to consult. <div eID="gen16398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16399" type="x-p"/> The understanding of the aged - זקנים zekenim signifies the same here as our word elders or elder-men; which includes in itself the two ideas of seniority, or considerably advanced age, and official authority. These can do no more to save a state which God designs to destroy, notwithstanding their great political wisdom and knowledge, than the child who can neither reason nor speak.
entries.901c875d6d3d391b7e0864f3acc639ca5f019f4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16400" type="x-p"/> He poureth contempt upon princes - נדיבים nedibim, "those of royal extraction;" widely different from the כהנים cohanim mentioned <reference osisRef="Job.12.19">Job 12:19</reference>. <div eID="gen16400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16401" type="x-p"/> Weakeneth the strength of the mighty - אפיקים aphikim, the compact; the well-strung together; the nervous and sinewy. Perhaps there is a reference here to the crocodile, as the same term is applied, <reference osisRef="Job.40.13">Job 40:13</reference>, to the compactness of his bones: and as רפה מזיח rippah meziach, which we translate weakeneth the strength, signifies more properly looseth the girdle, as the margin has properly rendered it, the reference seems still more pointed; for it is known that "the crocodile, from the shoulders to the extremity of the tail, is covered with large square scales, disposed like parallel girdles, fifty-two in number. In the middle of each girdle are four protuberances, which become higher as they approach the end of the tail, and compose four rows." See the quotation in Parkhurst, under the word אפק drow eh aphak. What is human strength against this? We may say as the Lord said, <reference osisRef="Job.40.19">Job 40:19</reference> : He that made him can make his sword to approach unto him. He alone can loose the girdles of this mighty one.
entries.407bf5d52c35b56fc8c155259dabf17c2f28328d: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16402" type="x-p"/> He discovereth deep things out of darkness - This may refer either to God's works in the great deep, or to the plots and stratagems of wicked men, conspiracies that were deeply laid, well digested, and about to be produced into existence, when death, whose shadow had hitherto concealed them, is to glut himself with carnage.
entries.9f4c54da11a06242afc3f352868a82efdc40e4c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen16402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16403" type="x-p"/> He increaseth the nations - Mr. Good translates, He letteth the nations grow licentious. Pride, fullness of bread, with extensive trade and commerce, produce luxury; and this is ever accompanied with profligacy of manners. When, then, the cup of this iniquity is full, God destroys the nation, by bringing or permitting to come against it a nation less pampered, more necessitous, and inured to toil. <div eID="gen16403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16404" type="x-p"/> He enlargeth the nations - Often permits a nation to acquire an accession of territory, and afterwards shuts them up within their ancient boundaries, and often contracts even those. All these things seem to occur as natural events, and the consequences of state intrigues, and such like causes; but when Divine inspiration comes to pronounce upon them, they are shown to be the consequence of God's acting in his judgment and mercy; for it is by him that kings reign; it is he who putteth down one and raiseth up another.
entries.db96101b5c9fff04c58d3d6f3f157d22a130a7ea: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen16404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16405" type="x-p"/> He taketh away the heart of the chief - Suddenly deprives the leaders of great counsels, or mighty armies of courage; so that, panic-struck, they flee when none pursueth, or are confounded when about to enter on the accomplishment of important designs. <div eID="gen16405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16406" type="x-p"/> And causeth them to wander in a wilderness - A plain allusion to the journeyings of the Israelites in the deserts of Arabia, on their way to the promised land. Their chief, Aaron, had his courage all taken away by the clamors of the people; and so made them a molten calf to be the object of their worship, which defection from God was the cause of their wandering nearly forty years in the trackless wilderness. The reference is so marked, that it scarcely admits of a doubt; yet Houbigant and some others have called it in question, and suppose that those chiefs or heads of families which led out colonies into distant parts are principally intended. It answers too well to the case of the Israelites in the wilderness to admit of any other interpretation.
entries.15776a907422c9027f66593b6d047916f6655956: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen16406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16407" type="x-p"/> They grope in the dark - The writer seems to have had his eye on those words of Moses, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.28">Deu 28:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.28.29">Deu 28:29</reference> : The Lord shall smite thee with madness, and blindness, and astonishment of heart; and thou shalt Grope At Noonday, as the Blind Gropeth In Darkness. And this also may refer to the unaccountable errors, transgressions, and judicial blindness of the Israelites in their journeying to the promised land: but it will apply also to the state of wicked nations under judicial blindness. The writer is principally indebted for his imagery, and indeed for the chief expressions used here, to <reference osisRef="Psa.107.27">Psa 107:27</reference> : They reel to and fro, and stagger like a drunken man. <reference osisRef="Psa.107.39">Psa 107:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.107.40">Psa 107:40</reference> : Again, they are minished and brought low through oppression, affliction, and sorrow. He Poureth Contempt Upon Princes, and Causeth Them To Wonder In The Wilderness, where there is No Way. Mr. Good has some judicious reflections on this chapter, particularly on <reference osisRef="Job.12.13-Job.12.22">Job 12:13-22</reference> : "It should be observed," says he, "that the entire passage has a reference to the machinery of a regular and political government; and that its general drift is to imprint on the mind of the hearer the important doctrine that the whole of the constituent principles of such a government, its officers and institutions; its monarchs and princes; its privy-counselors, judges, and ministers of state; its chieftains, public orators, and assembly of elders; its nobles, or men of hereditary rank; and its stout robust peasantry, as we should express it in the present day; nay, the deep designing villains that plot in secret its destruction; - that the nations themselves, and the heads or sovereigns of the nations, are all and equally in the hands of the Almighty: that with him human pomp is poverty; human excellence, turpitude; human judgment, error; human wisdom, folly; human dignity, contempt; human strength, weakness."  <chapter eID="Job.12"/> <div eID="gen16407" type="x-p"/>

entries.c36a75769f7c1634c3da54a9b6844e8982657691: <reference osisRef="Job.12.1-Job.3.1">Job 12:1-3   1</reference>  The Job began, and said:   2  Truly then ye are the people, <div eID="gen7304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7305" type="x-p"/> And wisdom shall die with you!   3  I also have a heart as well as you; <div eID="gen7305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7306" type="x-p"/> I do not stand behind you; <div eID="gen7306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7307" type="x-p"/> And to whom should not such things be known? <div eID="gen7307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7308" type="x-p"/> The admission, which is strengthened by כּי אמנם, truly then (distinct from אמנם כּי, for truly, <reference osisRef="Job.36.4">Job 36:4</reference>, similar to כּי הנּה, behold indeed, <reference osisRef="Ps.128.4">Psa 128:4</reference>), is intended as irony: ye are not merely single individuals, but the people = race of men (עם, as <reference osisRef="Isa.40.7">Isa 40:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.5">Isa 42:5</reference>), so that all human understanding is confined to you, and there is none other to be found; and when once you die, it will seem to have died out. The lxx correctly renders: μὴ ὑμεῖς ἐστὲ ἄνθρωποι μόνοι (according to the reading of the <hi type="italic">Cod. Alex.</hi>); he also has a heart like them, he is therefore not empty, נבוב, Job 11:12. Heart is, like <reference osisRef="Job.34.10">Job 34:10</reference>, comp. נלבב, <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference>, equivalent to νοῦς διάνοια; Ewald’s translation, “I also have a head even as you” (“brains” would better accord with the connection), is a western form of expression, and modern and unbiblical (vid., Division ”Herz und Haupt,” <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. iv. §12). He is not second to them; מן נפל, like <reference osisRef="Job.13.2">Job 13:2</reference>, properly to slip from, to be below any one; מן is not the comparative (Ewald). Oetinger’s translation is not bad: I cannot slink away at your presence. Who has not a knowledge of such things as those which they, by setting themselves up as defenders of God, have presented to him! אתּי היה is equivalent to ידעתּי, σύνοιδα, Isa 59:12.
entries.7e9f90af5dcc0591c6e3db9ccd9e77d38f033f2a: <reference osisRef="Job.12.4-Job.6.4">Job 12:4-6   4</reference>  I must be a mockery to my own friend, <div eID="gen7308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7309" type="x-p"/> I who called on Eloah and He heard me; <div eID="gen7309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7310" type="x-p"/> A mockery - the just, the godly man.   5  Contempt belongs to misfortune, according to the ideas of the prosperous; <div eID="gen7310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7311" type="x-p"/> It awaits those who are ready to slip.   6  Tents of the destroyer remain in peace, <div eID="gen7311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7312" type="x-p"/> And those that defy God are prosperous, <div eID="gen7312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7313" type="x-p"/> Who taketh Eloah into his hand. <div eID="gen7313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7314" type="x-p"/> The synallage of לרעהוּ for לרעי is not nearly so difficult as many others: a laughing-stock to his own friend; comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">Isa 2:8</reference>, they worship the work of their (his) own hands (ידיו). “One who called on Eloah (לאלוהּ, for which לאלוהּ is found in lxx at <reference osisRef="Job.36.2">Job 36:2</reference>) and He heard him” is in apposition to the subject; likewise תמים צדיק, which is to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Prov.11.5">Pro 11:5</reference>, צדיק (from צדק, Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣdq</hi>, to be hard, firm, stiff, straight), is one who in his conduct rules himself strictly according to the will of God; תמים, one whose thoughts are in all respects and without disguise what they should be-in one word: pure. Most old translators (Targ., Vulg., Luther) give לפּיד the signification, a torch. Thus e.g., Levi v. Gerson explains: “According to the view of the prosperous and carnally secure, he who is ready for falterings of the feet, i.e., likely to fall, is like a lighted torch which burns away and destroys whatever comes in contact with it, and therefore one keeps aloof from him; but it is also more than this: he is an object of contempt in their eyes.” Job might not inappropriately say, that in the eyes of the prosperous he is like a despised, cast-away torch (comp. the similar figure, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">Isa 14:19</reference>, like a branch that is rejected with contempt); and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.12.5">Job 12:5</reference></hi> would be suitably connected with this if למועדי could be derived from a substantive מעד, <hi type="italic">vacillatio</hi>, but neither the usage of the language nor the <hi type="italic">scriptio plena</hi> (after which Jerome translates <hi type="italic">tempus statutum,</hi> and consequently has in mind the מועדים, times of festal pilgrimages, which are also called ררלים in later times), nor the vowel pointing (instead of which מעדי would be expected), is favourable to this. רגל מועדי signifies <hi type="italic">vacillantes pede,</hi> those whose prosperity is shaken, and who are in danger of destruction that is near at hand. We therefore, like Abenezra and modern expositors, who are here happily agreed, take לפיד as composed of ל and פּיד, a word common to the books of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.30.24">Job 30:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.29">Job 31:29</reference>) and Proverbs (ch. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.22">Pro 24:22</reference>), which is compared by the Jewish lexicographers, according both to form and meaning, to כּיד (<reference osisRef="Job.21.20">Job 21:20</reference>) and איד, and perhaps signifies originally dissolution (comp. פדה), decease (Syr. <hi type="italic">f'jodo</hi>, escape; Arab. <hi type="italic">faid</hi>, dying), fall, then generally calamity, misfortune: contempt (befits) misfortune, according to the thoughts (or thinking), idea of the prosperous. The pointing wavers between לעשׁתּות and the more authorized לעשׁתּוּת, with which Parchon compares the nouns עבדוּת and מרדּוּת; the ת, like ד in the latter word, has <hi type="italic">Dag. lene,</hi> since the punctuation is in this respect not quite consistent, or follows laws at present unknown (comp.
