Ges. §21, rem. 2). <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.12.5">Job 12:5</reference></hi> is now suitably connected: ready (with reference to בוז) for those who stumble, i.e., contempt certainly awaits such, it is ready and waiting for them, נכון, ἕτοιμος, like Exo 34:2. <div eID="gen7314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7315" type="x-p"/> While the unfortunate, in spite of his innocence, has thus only to expect contempt, the tents, i.e., dwellings and possessions, of the oppressor and the marauder remain in prosperity; ישׁליוּ for ישׁלוּ, an intensive form used not only in pause (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>; comp. <reference osisRef="Deut.32.37">Deu 32:37</reference>) and with greater distinctives (Num 34:6; <reference osisRef="Ps.122.6">Psa 122:6</reference>), but also in passages where it receives no such accent (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.2">Psa 57:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.2">Psa 73:2</reference>). On אהלים, instead of אהלים, vid., Ges. §93, 6, 3. The verbal clause (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference></hi>) is followed by a substantival clause (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference></hi>). בּטּחות is an abstract plural from בּטּוּח, perfectly secure; therefore: the most care-less security is the portion of those who provoke God (lxx περοργίζουσι);<note placement="foot">Luther takes בטחות as the adverb to מרגיזי: <hi type="italic">und toben wider Gott thürstiglich</hi> (vid., Vilmar, Pastoraltheolog. Blätter, 1861, S. 110-112); according to the Vulg., <hi type="italic">et audacter provocant Deum</hi>.</note> and this is continued in an individualizing form: him who causes Eloah to go into his hand. Seb. Schmid explains this passage in the main correctly: <hi type="italic">qui Deum in manu fert h.e. qui manum aut potentiam suam pro Deo habet et licitum sibi putat quodlibet;</hi> comp. <reference osisRef="Hab.1.11">Hab 1:11</reference> : “this his strength becomes God to him,” i.e., he deifies his own power, and puts it in the place of God. But הביא signifies, in this connection with לידו (not בידו), neither to carry, nor to lead (Gesenius, who compares <reference osisRef="Ps.74.5">Psa 74:5</reference>, where, however, it signifies to cause to go into = to strike into); it must be translated: he who causes Eloah to enter into his hand; from which translation it is clear that not the deification of the hand, but of that which is taken into the hand, is meant. This which is taken into the hand is not, however, an idol (Abenezra), but the sword; therefore: him who thinks after the manner of Lamech,<note placement="foot">[Comp <hi type="italic">Pentateuch</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Gen.4.25">Gen 4:25</reference>, Clark’s Foreign Theological Library. - Tr.]</note> as he takes the iron weapon of attack and defence into his hand, that he needs no other God.
entries.340dccb31c1d9b5effe04d751c16dd354244a05a: <reference osisRef="Job.12.7-Job.10.7">Job 12:7-10   7</reference>  But ask now even the beasts - they shall teach it thee; <div eID="gen7315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7316" type="x-p"/> And the birds of heaven - they shall declare it to thee:   8  Or look thoughtfully to the ground - it shall teach it thee; <div eID="gen7316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7317" type="x-p"/> And the fish of the sea shall tell it thee.   9  Who would not recognise in all this <div eID="gen7317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7318" type="x-p"/> That the hand of Jehovah hath wrought this, 10  In whose hand is the soul of every living thing, <div eID="gen7318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7319" type="x-p"/> And the breath of all mankind?! <div eID="gen7319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7320" type="x-p"/> The meaning of the whole strophe is perverted if זאת (<reference osisRef="Job.12.9">Job 12:9</reference>), is, with Ewald, referred to “the destiny of severe suffering and pain,” and if that which precedes is accordingly referred to the testimony of creation to God as its author. Since, as a glance at what follows shows, Job further on praises God as the governor of the universe, it may be expected that the reference is here to God as the creator and preserver of the world, which seems to be the meaning of the words. Job himself expresses the purpose of this hymn of confession, Job 12:2., Job 13:1.: he will show the friends that the majesty of God, before which he ought, according to their demands, to humble himself in penitence, is not less known to him than to them; and with ואולם, <hi type="italic">verum enim vero</hi>, he passes over to this subject when he begins his third answer with the following thought: The perception in which you pride yourselves I also possess; true, I am an object of scornful contempt to you, who are as little able to understand the suffering of the godly as the prosperity of the godless, nevertheless what you know I also know: ask now, etc. Bildad had appealed to the sayings of the ancients, which have the long experience of the past in their favour, to support the justice of the divine government; Job here appeals to the absoluteness of the divine rule over creation. In form, this strophe is the counterpart of <reference osisRef="Job.8.8-Job.8.10">Job 8:8-10</reference> in the speech of Bildad, and somewhat also of <reference osisRef="Job.11.7-Job.11.9">Job 11:7-9</reference> in that of Zophar. The working of God, which infinitely transcends human power and knowledge, is the sermon which is continuously preached by all created things; they all proclaim the omnipotence and wisdom of the Creator. <div eID="gen7320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7321" type="x-p"/> The plural בּהמות is followed by the verb that refers to it, in the singular, in favour of which <reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Gen 49:22</reference> is the favourite example among old expositors (Ges. §146, 3). On the other hand, the verb might follow the collective עוף in the <hi type="italic">plural</hi>, according to Ges. §146, 1. The plural, however, is used only in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.12.8">Job 12:8</reference></hi>, because there the verb precedes instead of following its subject. According to the rule Ges. §128, 2, the jussive form of the fut. follows the imperative. In the midst of this enumeration of created things, שׂיח, as a substantive, seems to signify the plants - and especially as Arab. <hi type="italic">šı̂h</hi> even now, in the neighbourhood of Job’s ancient habitation, is the name of a well-known mountain-plant - under whose shade a meagre vegetation is preserved even in the hot season (vid., on Job 30:4.). But (1) שׂיח as subst. is <hi type="italic">gen. masc.</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.2.5">Gen 2:5</reference>); (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.2">2</reference>) instead of לערץ, in order to describe a plant that is found on the ground, or one rooted in the ground, it must be על־הארץ or בארץ;   (3) the mention of plants between the birds and fishes would be strange. It may therefore be taken as the imperative: speak to the earth (lxx, Targ., Vulg., and most others); or, which I prefer, since the Aramaic construction לו סח, <hi type="italic">narravit ei,</hi> does not occur elsewhere in Hebrew (although perhaps <hi type="italic">implicite,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.6.22">Pro 6:22</reference>, תשׂיחך = לך תשׂיח, <hi type="italic">favulabitur</hi>, or <hi type="italic">confabulabitur tibi</hi>), as a pregnant expression: think, i.e., look meditatively to the earth (Ewald), since שׂוּח (שׂיח), like הגה, combines the significations of quiet or articulate meditation on a subject. The exhortation directs attention not to the earth in itself, but to the small living things which move about on the ground, comprehended in the collective name רמשׂ, syn. שׁרץ (creeping things), in the record of creation. All these creatures, though without reason and speech, still utter a language which is heard by every intelligent man. Renan, after Ewald, translates erroneously: <hi type="italic">qui ne sait parmi tous ces êtres.</hi> They do not even possess knowledge, but they offer instruction, and are a means of knowledge; בּ with ידע, like <reference osisRef="Gen.15.8">Gen 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.42.33">Gen 42:33</reference>, and freq. All the creatures named declare that the hand of Jehovah has made “this,” whatever we see around us, τὸ βλεπόμενον, Heb 11:3. In the same manner in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.2">Isa 66:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.22">Jer 14:22</reference>, כּל־אלּה is used of the world around us. In the hand of God, i.e., in His power, because His workmanship, are the souls of all living things, and the spirit (that which came direct from God) of all men; every order of life, high and low, owes its origin and continuance to Him. אישׁ is the individual, and in this connection, in which נפשׁ and רוּח (= נשׁמה) are certainly not unintentionally thus separated, the individual man. Creation is the school of knowledge, and man is the learner. And this knowledge forces itself upon one’s attention: <hi type="italic">quis non cognoverit?</hi> The <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. has this subjunctive force also elsewhere in interrogative clauses, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.11.3">Psa 11:3</reference> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Gen.21.7">Gen 21:7</reference>). That the name of God, JEHOVAH, for once escapes the poet here, is to be explained from the phrase “the hand of Jehovah hath made this,” being a somewhat proverbial expression (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.41.20">Isa 41:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.2">Isa 66:2</reference>). <div eID="gen7321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7322" type="x-p"/> Job now refers to the sayings of the fathers, the authority of which, as being handed down from past generations, Bildad had maintained in his opposition to Job.
entries.b0e52bfb2e738aa819b61067647d2fa79b0a183e: <reference osisRef="Job.12.11-Job.13.11">Job 12:11-13 11</reference>  Shall not the ear try sayings, <div eID="gen7322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7323" type="x-p"/> As the palate tasteth food? 12  Among the ancients is wisdom, <div eID="gen7323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7324" type="x-p"/> And long life is understanding. 13  With Him is wisdom and strength; <div eID="gen7324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7325" type="x-p"/> Counsel and understanding are His. <div eID="gen7325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7326" type="x-p"/> The meaning of <reference osisRef="Job.12.11">Job 12:11</reference> is, that the sayings (מלּין, <reference osisRef="Job.8.10">Job 8:10</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.5.27">Job 5:27</reference>) of the ancients are not to be accepted without being proved; the <hi type="italic">waw</hi> in וחך is <hi type="italic">waw</hi> <hi type="italic">adaequationis</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Job.5.7">Job 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference>, therefore equivalent to <hi type="italic">quemadmodum</hi>; it places together for comparison things that are analogous: The ear, which is used here like αἰθητήριον (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.14">Heb 5:14</reference>), has the task of searching out and testing weighty sayings, as the palate by tasting has to find out delicious and suitable food; this is indicated by לו, the <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi>. So far Job recognises the authority of these traditional sayings. At any rate, he adds (<reference osisRef="Job.12.12">Job 12:12</reference>): wisdom is to be expected from the hoary-headed, and length of life is understanding, i.e., it accompanies length of life. “Length of days” may thus be taken as the subject (Ewald, Olsh.); but בּ may also, with the old translations and expositors, be carried forward from the preceding clause: ἐν δὲ πολλῷ βίῳ ἐπιστήμη (lxx). We prefer, as the most natural: long life is a school of understanding. But - such is the antithesis in <reference osisRef="Job.12.13">Job 12:13</reference> which belongs to this strophe - the highest possessor of wisdom, as of might, is God. Ewald inserts two self-made couplets before <reference osisRef="Job.12.12">Job 12:12</reference>, which in his opinion are required both by the connection and “the structure of the strophe;” we see as little need for this interpolation here as before, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job 6:14</reference></hi>. עמּו and לו, which are placed first for the sake of emphasis, manifestly introduce an antithesis; and it is evident from the antithesis, that the One who is placed in contrast to the many men of experience is God. Wisdom is found among the ancients, although their sayings are not to be always implicitly accepted; but wisdom belongs to God as an attribute of His nature, and indeed absolutely, i.e., on every side, and without measure, as the piling up of synonymous expressions implies: חכמה, which perceives the reason of the nature, and the reality of the existence, of things; עצה, which is never perplexed as to the best way of attaining its purpose; תּבוּנה, which can penetrate to the bottom of what is true and false, sound and corrupt (comp. 1Ki 3:9); and also גּבוּרה, which is able to carry out the plans, purposes, and decisions of this wisdom against all hindrance and opposition. <div eID="gen7326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7327" type="x-p"/> In the strophe which follows, from his own observation and from traditional knowledge (<reference osisRef="Job.13.1">Job 13:1</reference>), Job describes the working of God, as the unsearchably wise and the irresistibly mighty One, both among men and in nature.
entries.6a45981cd066d22815faf2a2f34030236a7e5e86: Job 12:14-16 14  Behold, He breaketh down and it cannot be built again, <div eID="gen7327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7328" type="x-p"/> He shutteth up, and it cannot be opened. 15  Behold, He restraineth the waters and they dry up, <div eID="gen7328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7329" type="x-p"/> And He letteth them out and they overturn the earth. 16  With Him is might and existence, <div eID="gen7329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7330" type="x-p"/> The erring and the deceiver are His. <div eID="gen7330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7331" type="x-p"/> God is almighty, and everything in opposition to Him powerless. If He break down (any structure whatever), it can never be rebuilt; should He close upon any one (i.e., the dungeon, as perhaps a cistern covered with a stone, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.53">Lam 3:53</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Jer.38.6">Jer 38:6</reference>; על with reference to the depth of the dungeon, instead of the usual בּעד), it (that which is closed from above) cannot be opened again. In like manner, when He desires to punish a land, He disposes the elements according to His will and pleasure, by bringing upon it drought or flood. יעצר, <hi type="italic">coercet</hi>, according to the correct Masoretic mode of writing יעצר with dagesh in the Ssade, in order clearly to distinguish in the pronunciation between the forms <hi type="italic">j'a-ssor</hi> and <hi type="italic">jaa'ssor</hi> (יעצר);<note placement="foot">Vid., my notice of Bär’s <hi type="italic">Psalter-Ausgabe</hi>, <hi type="italic">Luth. Zeitschr</hi>. 1863, 3; and comp. Keil on <reference osisRef="Lev.4.13">Lev 4:13</reference> (<hi type="italic">Comm on Pent</hi>., Clark’s transl.).</note> ויבשׁוּ (for which Abulwalid writes ויבשׁוּ) is a defective form of writing according to Ges. §69, 3, 3; the form ויהפכוּ with the similarly pointed <hi type="italic">fut. consec.,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.12">1Sa 25:12</reference>, form a pair (zuwg) noted by the Masora. By תּוּשׁיּה, which is ascribed to God, is here to be understood that which really exists, the real, the objective, knowledge resting on an objective actual basis, in contrast with what only appears to be; so that consequently the idea of <reference osisRef="Job.12.16">Job 12:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.12.13">Job 12:13</reference> is somewhat veiled; for the primary notion of חכמה is thickness, solidity, purity, like πυκνότης.<note placement="foot">The primary notion of חכם, Arab. <hi type="italic">hkm</hi>, is, to be thick, firm, solid, as the prim. notion of Arab. <hi type="italic">sachfa</hi> (to be foolish, silly) is to be thin, loose, not holding together (as a bad texture). The same fundamental notions are represented in the expression of moral qualities (in distinction from intellectual) by צדק, Arab. <hi type="italic">sdq</hi>, and רשׁע, (Arab. <hi type="italic">rs'</hi>, <hi type="italic">rsg</hi>).</note> <div eID="gen7331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7332" type="x-p"/> This strophe closes like the preceding, which favours our division. The line with עמּו is followed by one with לו, which affirms that, in the supremacy of His rule and the wisdom of His counsels, God makes evil in every form subservient to His designs.
entries.983308065ad83f007970a6552ba98b9092227cd7: Job 12:17-21 17  He leadeth away counsellors stripped of their robes, <div eID="gen7332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7333" type="x-p"/> And maketh judges fools. 18  The authority of kings He looseth, <div eID="gen7333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7334" type="x-p"/> And bindeth their loins with bands. 19  He leadeth away priests stripped of their robes, <div eID="gen7334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7335" type="x-p"/> And overthroweth those who are firmly established. 20  He removeth the speech of the eloquent, <div eID="gen7335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7336" type="x-p"/> And taketh away the judgment of the aged. 21  He poureth contempt upon princes, <div eID="gen7336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7337" type="x-p"/> And maketh loose the girdle of the mighty. <div eID="gen7337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7338" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.12.17">Job 12:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.12.19">Job 12:19</reference>, שׁולל is added to מוליך as a conditional accusative; the old expositors vary in the rendering of this word; at any rate it does not mean: chained (Targ. on <reference osisRef="Job.12.17">Job 12:17</reference>), from שׁלל (שׁרר), which is reduplicated in the word שׁלשׁלת, a chain, a word used in later Hebrew than the language of the Old Testament (שׁרשׁרה is the Old Testament word); nor is it: taken as booty, made captive (lxx αἰχμαλώτους; Targ. on <reference osisRef="Job.12.19">Job 12:19</reference>, בּבזתא, in the quality of spoil) = משׁולל; but it is a neuter adjective closely allied to the idea of the verb, <hi type="italic">exutus</hi>, not however <hi type="italic">mente</hi> (deprived of sense), but vestibus; not merely barefooted (Hirz., Oehler, with lxx, Mic 1:8, ἀνυπόδετος), which is the meaning of יחף, but: stripped of their clothes with violence (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.20.4">Isa 20:4</reference>), stripped in particular of the insignia of their power. He leads them half-naked into captivity, and takes away the judges as fools (יהולל, vid., Psychol. S. 292), by destroying not only their power, but the prestige of their position also. We find echoes of this utterance respecting God’s paradoxical rule in the world in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.23">Isa 40:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.25">Isa 44:25</reference>; and Isaiah’s oracle on Egypt, <reference osisRef="Job.19.11-Job.19.15">Job 19:11-15</reference>, furnishes an illustration in the reality. <div eID="gen7338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7339" type="x-p"/> It is but too natural to translate <reference osisRef="Job.12.18">Job 12:18</reference> : the bands of kings He looses (after <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Psa 116:16</reference>, למוסרי פתחת, Thou hast loosed my bands); but the relation of the two parts of the verse can then not be this: He unchains and chains kings (Hirz., Ew., Heiligst. Schlottm.), for the <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> ויּאסר requires a contrast that is intimately connected with the context, and not of mere outward form: fetters in which kings have bound others (מלכים, <hi type="italic">gen. subjectivus</hi>) He looses, and binds <hi type="italic">them</hi> in fetters (Raschi), - an explanation which much commends itself, if מוּסר could only be justified as the construct of מוּסר by the remark that “the <hi type="italic">o</hi> sinks into <hi type="italic">u</hi>” (Ewald, §213, <hi type="italic">c</hi>). מוּסר does not once occur in the signification <hi type="italic">vinculum</hi>; but only the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. מוסרים and מוסרות, <hi type="italic">vincula</hi>, accord with the usage of the language, so that even the pointing מוסר proposed by Hirzel is a venture. מוּסר, however, as constr. of מוּסר, correction, discipline, rule (i.e., as the domination of punishment, from יסר, <hi type="italic">castigare</hi>), is an equally suitable sense, and is probably connected by the poet with פּתּח (a word very familiar to him, <reference osisRef="Job.30.11">Job 30:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.39.5">Job 39:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.41.6">Job 41:6</reference>) on account of its relation both in sound and sense to מוסרים (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.105.22">Psa 105:22</reference>). The English translation is correct: <hi type="italic">He looseth the authority of kings.</hi> The antithesis is certainly lost, but the thoughts here moreover flow on in synonymous parallelism.
entries.e4b0d085d99462766f31ae1d9dcf0f9ab7fd7fbc: Job 12:22-25 22  He discovereth deep things out of darkness, <div eID="gen7340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7341" type="x-p"/> And bringeth out to light the shadow of death; 23  He giveth prosperity to nations and then destroyeth them, <div eID="gen7341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7342" type="x-p"/> Increase of territory to nations and then carrieth them away; 24  He taketh away the understanding of the chief people of the land, <div eID="gen7342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7343" type="x-p"/> And maketh them to wander in a trackless wilderness; 25  They grope in darkness without light, <div eID="gen7343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7344" type="x-p"/> He maketh them to stagger like a drunken man. <div eID="gen7344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7345" type="x-p"/> The meaning of <reference osisRef="Job.12.22">Job 12:22</reference> in this connection can only be, that there is nothing so finely spun out that God cannot make it visible. All secret plans of the wicked, all secret sins, and the deeds of the evil-doer though veiled in deep darkness, He bringeth before the tribunal of the world. The form of writing given by the Masora is עמוּקות with <hi type="italic">koph raphatum</hi>, consequently plur. from עמוּק, like ערוּמים, עצוּמים from ערוּם, עצוּם, not from עמק.<note placement="foot">Kimchi in his Wörterbuch adopts the form עמקּות, but gives Abulwalid as an authority for the lengthened form, which, according to the Masora on <reference osisRef="Lev.13.3">Lev 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.25">Lev 13:25</reference>, is the traditional. The two exceptions where the form occurs with a long vowel are <reference osisRef="Prov.23.27">Pro 23:27</reference> and this passage.</note> <div eID="gen7345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7346" type="x-p"/> The lxx translates משגיא πλανῶν, as it is also explained in several Midrash-passages, but only by a few Jewish expositors (Jachja, Alschech) by מטעה. The word, however, is not משׁגּיא, but משׂגּיא with ש <hi type="italic">sinistrum</hi>, after which in Midrash Esther it is explained by מגדיל; and Hirzel correctly interprets it of upward growth (Jerome after the Targ. unsuitably, <hi type="italic">multiplicat</hi>), and שׁטח, on the other hand, of growth in extent. The latter word is falsely explained by the Targ. in the sense of <hi type="italic">expandere rete</hi>, and Abenezra also falsely explains: He scatters nations, and brings them to their original peace. The verb שׁטח is here connected with ל, as הפתּה (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.27">Gen 9:27</reference>); both signify to make a wider and longer space for any one, used here of the ground where they dwell and rule. The opposite, in an unpropitious sense, is הנחה, which is used here, as 2Ki 18:11, in a similar sense with הגלה (<hi type="italic">abducere</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">in</hi> <hi type="italic">servitutem</hi>). We have intentionally translated גוים nations, עם people; for גּוי, as we shall show elsewhere, is the mass held together by the ties of a common origin, language, and country; (עם) עם, the people bound together by unity of government, whose <hi type="italic">membra praecipua</hi> are consequently called העם ראשׁי. הארץ is, in this connection, the country, although elsewhere, as <reference osisRef="Isa.24.4">Isa 24:4</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.42.5">Job 42:5</reference>, הארץ עם signifies also the people of the earth or mankind; for the Hebrew language expresses a country as a portion of the earth, and the earth as a whole, by the same name. Job dwells longer on this tragic picture, how God makes the star of the prosperity of these chiefs to set in mad and blind self-destruction, according to the proverb, <hi type="italic">quem Deus perdere vult prius dementat.</hi> This description seems to be echoed in many points in Isaiah, especially in the oracle on Egypt, Job 19 (e.g., כּשּׁכּור, <reference osisRef="Job.19.14">Job 19:14</reference>). The connection ברך לא בתהו is not genitival; but דרך לא is either an adverbial clause appended to the verb, as חקר לא, <reference osisRef="Job.34.24">Job 34:24</reference>, בנים לא, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.30">1Ch 2:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.32">1Ch 2:32</reference>, or, which we prefer as being more natural, and on account of the position of the words, a virtual adjective: in a trackless waste, as אישׁ לא, <reference osisRef="Job.38.26">Job 38:26</reference>; עבות לא,   <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference> (Olsh.). <div eID="gen7346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7347" type="x-p"/> Job here takes up the tone of Eliphaz (comp. Job 5:13.). Intentionally he is made to excel the friends in a recognition of the absolute majesty of God. He is not less cognizant of it than they.  <chapter eID="Job.12"/> <div eID="gen7347" type="x-p"/>
